country.comment: Explicitly focused on the urban water and sanitation sector in Peru.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title and Resumen; PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF p. 3, Introduction

effect_estimate.comment: Purely descriptive secondary statistical and regulatory analysis with no inferential regression, confidence intervals, or p-values; Figures 1–8 are embedded graphics described in text alongside Tables 1–2.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive secondary benchmarking findings only (no inferential statistical effect estimate reported): across Peru's 50–51 urban sanitation service providers (EPS), SUNASS reported that 3.3 million Peruvians lack access to a public drinking water network and 6.4 million lack sewerage connections (urban coverage peaked in 2017 at 92.5% for drinking water and 85.9% for sewerage before slightly regressing, leaving approximately 2 million urban inhabitants without drinking water and 3 million without sewerage); service continuity and pressure remain low in several utilities (e.g., 6 hours/day and 6 m.c.a. in SEDAJULIACA; 3.7 hours/day in EMAPAVIGS; <7 m.c.a. in SEDALIB, EPS Grau, and EPSEL), average drinking water losses reach 37% across the 50 EPS (31.4% in SEDAPAL vs. 42% in the other 49 EPS), micrometering covers 75% of users (60% excluding SEDAPAL), the weighted average tariff is S/ 2.941 per m3, pipe breaks totaled 17,524 events in 2022 (down from 22,101 in 2017), and 443,673 operational and commercial complaints were registered in 2022, with approximately 10% of users complaining at least once per year despite burdensome in-person procedures.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 1–2, Resumen/Abstract; PDF pp. 5–12, Results (Tables 1–2, Figures 1–8 text); PDF pp. 13–14, Conclusions

mechanism_certainty.comment: Non-experimental descriptive study (ceiling <= 2). Although the paper reports aggregate univariate SUNASS benchmarking counts for complaints (443,673 in 2022; ~10% of users), tariffs (S/ 2.941/m3), and service deficits (coverage, continuity, pipe breaks), it performs no statistical test or bivariate cross-tabulation linking regulatory/complaint mechanisms to service outcomes, nor does it empirically observe complaint handling or user deterrence; the claims that complaints serve as an indicator of management improvement and that tedious in-person protocols/queues deter users from complaining are posited/inferred by the author.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 4–12, Materiales y Métodos and Resultados; PDF pp. 13–14, Conclusiones

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines the user complaints process (443,673 operational and commercial complaints), the procedural burden of filing complaints in person (time-consuming protocols, multiple office visits, queues) as well as regulatory metering/billing procedures, and regulated water tariff levels/rules.
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 1–2, Resumen/Abstract; PDF p. 6, Results; PDF pp. 9–10, Figures 5–6 text; PDF p. 12, Figure 8 text; PDF p. 14, Conclusions

outcome_flags.comment: Reports descriptive benchmarking data on public water and sewerage network connections, population without water and sanitation access, urban coverage rates, hours of daily water continuity, water pressure and pipe-break reliability, and overall quality of sanitation service provision. Tariffs are discussed in terms of utility revenue sufficiency rather than household affordability.

outcome_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 1–4, Resumen/Abstract, Introduction, and Table 1; PDF pp. 5–11, Results (Table 2, Figures 1–4 and 7 text); PDF pp. 13–14, Conclusions

publication_year.where_found: PDF p. 1, journal header; PDF p. 15, article dates footer

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: The study combines documentary review of Peru's water and sanitation regulatory norms (tariff regulation, service quality regulation, Works for Taxes investment rules, billing/metering rules, and complaint protocols) with univariate descriptive regulatory benchmarking statistics across urban utilities, without an analytical cross-sectional exposure-outcome sample/regression, qualitative fieldwork, quasi-experimental comparator, or systematic literature search; Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework best fits this descriptive regulatory-institutional empirical design.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF pp. 1–2, Resumen/Abstract; PDF pp. 4–5, Materiales y Métodos

sample_size.comment: The text refers both to 51 urban companies (50 municipal + 1 state-owned SEDAPAL, pp. 1–3) and to 50 EPS in the national benchmarking breakdown (Table 1: 1 + 5 + 14 + 15 + 15 = 50 EPS, pp. 3–4, 8–9, 11), alongside 443,673 registered user complaints in 2022 (p. 12).
sample_size.value: 50–51 urban water and sanitation service providers (Entidades Prestadoras de Servicios de Saneamiento, EPS; stated as 51 urban companies in Abstract/p. 3 and 50 EPS in Table 1 and benchmarking summaries), with 443,673 registered operational and commercial complaints in 2022
sample_size.where_found: PDF pp. 1–2, Resumen/Abstract; PDF pp. 3–4, Introduction and Table 1; PDF p. 12, Figure 8 text

study_design.comment: Described by the author as basic, quantitative, non-experimental, descriptive research using documentary analysis of water/sanitation regulations and secondary descriptive benchmarking statistics; no analytical statistical modeling or primary survey/interview data collection was conducted.
study_design.value: Non-experimental descriptive documentary and secondary statistical benchmarking study
